messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm not sure what these warning messages mean and I've encountered them once before (see previous email "Warning messages: 1: In sqrt(1/diag(V)) 2: cov2cor(OUT[[b]])") .

What do they mean? Can I interpret my results?

Attached is the LDSC data and code for my bifactor model (where I added residual correlations between AUD and OCD to improve model fit) to reproduce the error.

Thank you!

Camille

LDSCoutput <- readRDS("ldsc.rds")

GWISmodel <- 'Internalizing =~  Neff_Meta_Dep + Neff_Meta_PTSD + Neff_Meta_OCD  + Neff_Meta_SH + Neff_Meta_Eat_Rev + Neff_Meta_ANX
                   Thought_Disorder =~ a*Neff_Meta_SCZ + a*Neff_Meta_BPD
                   Externalizing =~ b*Other.Substance.Hazard.Dependence_Neff + b*Neff_Meta_AUD

                   P =~  Neff_Meta_Dep + Neff_Meta_PTSD  + Neff_Meta_SH + Neff_Meta_Eat_Rev + Neff_Meta_OCD+
                   Neff_Meta_ANX + Neff_Meta_SCZ+ Neff_Meta_BPD + Other.Substance.Hazard.Dependence_Neff + Neff_Meta_AUD

                  Internalizing ~~ 0*Thought_Disorder
                  Externalizing ~~ 0*Internalizing
                  Thought_Disorder ~~ 0*Externalizing

                   P ~~ 0*Thought_Disorder
                   P ~~ 0*Internalizing
                   P ~~ 0*Externalizing

                   Neff_Meta_OCD ~~ Neff_Meta_AUD

                  Neff_Meta_Dep ~~ c*Neff_Meta_Dep
                  c > 0.000001 '

GWISoutput<-usermodel(covstruc = LDSCoutput, estimation = "DWLS",
                      model = GWISmodel, CFIcalc = TRUE,
                      imp_cov = T)

GWISoutput

messages.subject: Re: Warning Messages 1: In sqrt(1/diag(V)) : NaNs produced 2: In cov2cor(OUT[[b]]) :
messages.subject_clean: Warning Messages 1: In sqrt(1/diag(V)) : NaNs produced 2: In cov2cor(OUT[[b]]) :
messages.body_plain:
Hi Camille,

That warning is popping up in this case because of the constraint you are having to put on the residual variance in depression to keep it above 0 (warning goes away when you remove the constraint). The way I think about this situation is the warning is cueing you into an issue with the estimates resulting from the constraint and so the question is how much results shift with and without the constraint in the model. I would say a quick look at the standardized factor loadings in the model with and without the constraint indicates that results do shift quite a bit and so I would lean towards not trusting these model results.

I also typically like to use unit variance identification when working with two-indicator latents as the loadings are otherwise both fixed to 1 with the equality constraint. When I tried that out the models were failing to converge, which to my mind further indicates some instability in this model specification.

It already looks like you've done some careful modeling here with the residual covariance included, the orthogonal relationships among the three factors specified, equality constraints in the model, and constraints on the negative residual. All that to say I imagine it may be difficult to troubleshoot this model too much more as it seems like you've already done a lot of that work. Possible issues that stand out here are that there are two, two-indicator latents, that would be good to get a third indicator for if possible (of course two-indicator latents are fine it just may be causing convergence issues here) and the bifactor p-factor soaking up additional variance on top of everything else that is pushing something like MDD, that already has a really high rg of .9 with ANX, to have a negative residual. You could consider a hierarchical specification of p as an alternative, consider bringing in other variables, or try alternative specifications of this bifactor model.

Best,
 Andrew

On Tuesday, November 8, 2022 at 4:07:04 PM UTC-5 agro...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Jeff,
>
> These are great questions. I would say we are still in the phase of figuring out what warnings require filtering out results entirely. Since enrich is fixing the factor loadings from the genome-wide annotation, running the models within an annotation won't be exactly equivalent since those are going to freely estimate all of those loadings. That being said, I think it was good troubleshooting to still take a look at some of these individual annotations to ensure that model results within an annotation look relatively normal and the model still fits well.
>
> I would say if you are examining enrichment of factor variances, the warning about negative lv variances should generally be used to prune out results as this warning indicates latent variables with variances below 0. If the warning is about lavaan WARNING: covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite, I would not examine enrichment of the factor correlations since this warning often indicates model results with factor correlations > 1.
>
> Best,
>   Andrew
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm running a UserGWAS (6 traits - 2 factors). When running the model without SNPs I ran into some high loadings close to/over 1. I was able to fix that with a model constraint for two indicators, solving the issue of negative variances. However, this problem came back when running the model with SNPS. I have ~6 million SNPs, so I split the SNP list into six (~1 million SNPs each). However, one of these files, more specifically 345 SNPs, returned a warning about some estimated ov variances being negative.

I decided to run the model again, but now only with these 345 SNPs. I was surprised to see that it ran without any errors or warnings. The estimates and p-values for those SNPs also changed. I also tried re-running other small sets of SNPs to make sure I was running the exact same model, and these showed the same estimates and p-values as before. So, this brings me to two questions:

1. If each SNP is independent of each other, how is it possible that the warnings only show up when running them together with other SNPs?

2. Again, considering that each SNP is independent, would it be okay then to ignore the estimates with the warnings and just consider the new ones that ran without warnings?

Here is the piece of code I used:

load(file="LDSCoutput_6.RData")

model = 'F1 =~ SSEEK + RISK + EXTR
F2 =~ PURG + BIS + PREMED
F1~~F2
F1 ~ SNP
F2 ~ SNP
SSEEK ~~ a*SSEEK
a > .001
PREMED ~~ b*PREMED
b > .001'

gwas = userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput, SNPs = sumstats, model = model, std.lv <http://std.lv> = T, sub=c("F1~SNP", "F2~SNP"), parallel = T, cores = 15)

Best,
Dener

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dener,

Thanks for reaching out about this. My best guess as to why you are seeing different results for these SNPs depending on whether you use a full set of SNPs or just the 345 is because the first SNP run is used to produce starting values for all subsequent SNPs. This helps ease model convergence and speed-up run times when running as many models as there are SNPs in your dataset.

Generally speaking, I do not expect which SNP is first to affect results in any meaningful way. This is why you reassuringly see the same estimates when running in small batches for the SNPs that did not produce warnings. This is with the exception that SNPs that produce more unstable model results (e.g., with the negative residual variances you are seeing for these 345) may be more likely to converge on different, presumably local, solutions depending on the start values.

So to summarize, it sounds like if you let the model choose start values based on one of these 345 SNPs that it allows the model to converge on a more sensible solution as compared to start values from the other SNPs. Running these 345 SNPs on their own and using those estimates I would say is a reasonable troubleshooting strategy here. However, if these 345 SNPs do not produce significant effects on your two factors I might just drop them as it seems like they are more generally producing unstable estimates.

If they are producing significant effects on the factors, I would suggest two additional sanity checks to make sure these are credible results. First, I would confirm that this isn't a sharp deviation from the data going in by confirming that the Z-statistics for the factor indicators are relatively large in the sumstats output. Second, I would suggest setting the smooth_check argument to TRUE and try rerunning these 345 again to confirm that these aren't SNPs that require a high degree of smoothing of the genetic covariance matrix (I generally recommend removing SNPs with Zs in this smooth_check column > 1.96).

Best,
  Andrew
